prompt: Put Renata’s pre-arrival list in order, from acceptance to day one.
items: A welcome message saying what the first week looks like
Buddy chosen and first task written up
A short message from the buddy
Everything working before 9:00 on day one

prompt: Why did Renata take a third of Paula’s planned work out of the sprint for Lucas’s first two weeks?

choices.text: Paula was behind
choices.why: Nothing says so; the time was for Lucas.

choices.text: Otherwise the new person stops asking
choices.why: Right: being a buddy is work, and it needs time set aside.

choices.text: Because Paula would be handing over the reminder service to Lucas anyway during those two weeks
choices.why: The handover was a reason to choose Paula, not the reason to free her time.

choices.text: Company policy
choices.why: Not mentioned.

prompt: Which properties did Renata’s choice of first task have? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Real: finishing it would matter to somebody
choices.why: Yes: a clinic had reported it.

choices.text: Hard enough to test whether the hire was right
choices.why: No: the first task is not a test.

choices.text: Written up, so he could start without a briefing
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Small enough to reach production in the first week
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: In the area he would own
choices.why: Yes: the reminder service.

prompt: What is the one goal of a new engineer’s first week, by the lesson?

choices.text: Reading all the documentation
choices.why: Reading supports the goal; it is not the goal.

choices.text: Meeting everybody in the company, including the other teams the person will depend on later
choices.why: Introductions support the goal too.

choices.text: A small, real change of theirs reaches production
choices.why: Right: it proves the setup end to end, teaches the real process and makes them part of the team.

choices.text: Passing a technical assessment
choices.why: That happened before the offer.

prompt: On which day of his first week did Lucas’s first change reach production?
Why did Renata tell Lucas, in his first week, which area the hiring panel had flagged?
hint: Explicit from the start, with support.

choices.text: So the expectation was explicit and came with support, instead of surfacing in a review later
choices.why: Right: it avoids the surprise lesson 8 warned about.

choices.text: To warn him that he was on probation
choices.why: Nothing about probation; it came with a plan to help.

choices.text: Because the law requires interview feedback
choices.why: No legal requirement is mentioned.

choices.text: To lower his expectations of how fast he could expect to be promoted at Caju
choices.why: Promotion is not part of it.

prompt: A new hire has stopped asking questions in their third week. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: A reason to ask, not to confront.

choices.text: Ask a question with edges in the one-to-one
choices.why: Right: for example, the most confusing part of the codebase so far.

choices.text: Assume they are settled
choices.why: Silence usually means they asked and felt slow.

choices.text: Tell them to ask more questions, in front of the team, so that everybody hears it is welcome
choices.why: A public instruction adds pressure; the lesson suggests a question in private.

choices.text: Start a performance conversation
choices.why: Far too early, and not what the sign means.

prompt: What does each row of Lucas’s three-month plan include besides what is expected?

choices.text: A salary review date
choices.why: Not part of the plan.

choices.text: The name of the person who will replace him if he falls behind
choices.why: Nothing like that.

choices.text: A list of the courses he should complete in his own time to keep up with the team
choices.why: Not in the plan.

choices.text: How anybody will know
choices.why: Right: a measurable outcome lets a check-in say on track or behind.

prompt: Match each stage of Lucas’s plan with what was expected by then.

pairs.right: several fixes shipped; knows the deploy and the alerts
owns the reminder service day to day; shadowed one on-call week
led a small piece of the confirmations work; on the on-call rota

prompt: At thirty days, Lucas was behind on alerts because there had been no incident to learn from. What did they do?
hint: Changing a plan is not a failure.

choices.text: Moved it to the shadow week
choices.why: Right: the plan adapted to what happened, rather than inventing an exercise.

choices.text: Recorded it as a performance concern
choices.why: Nothing about it was a performance problem.

choices.text: Triggered a fake incident in production so he could practise responding to a real alert
choices.why: Not what they did; they used the shadow week.

choices.text: Dropped alerts from the plan
choices.why: They moved it, not dropped it.

prompt: A manager sees at thirty days that a new hire is well behind for reasons unrelated to onboarding, and decides to “give them time to settle in” before saying anything. What does the lesson say?
hint: The kindest-sounding version of a failure.

choices.text: Waiting is right during the first ninety days, which exist precisely so that people can adjust
choices.why: The plan exists to make problems visible early, not to postpone them.

choices.text: The hire was a mistake and should be reversed
choices.why: That is a decision lessons 19 to 21 approach carefully, not at thirty days on instinct.

choices.text: HR should handle it
choices.why: The manager has the conversation; HR may support.

choices.text: It is lesson 10’s failure in a kind disguise; new people are the ones who most need to hear it plainly
choices.why: Right: they have the least context to notice it themselves.

prompt: Put the three steps of the first on-call shift in order.
hint: Watch, act with a net, act alone with a backup.
trap: Going straight to primary is how Thiago ended up alone at 3 a.m. with an alert nobody had explained.

prompt: In a reverse-shadow week, who acts on a page?
hint: The roles are reversed from shadowing.

choices.text: The new person makes the calls, while the experienced engineer watches and stays ready to step in
choices.why: Right: the new person makes the decisions, with a safety net.

choices.text: The experienced engineer
choices.why: That is shadowing.

choices.text: Whoever answers the page first, since both people are paged at the same moment in that week
choices.why: The roles are defined in advance; the new person acts.

choices.text: The manager
choices.why: The manager is not on the rota for this.

prompt: What has to be true of every alert before a new person can be on call alone?

choices.text: It fires at least once a week
choices.why: Frequency is not the requirement.

choices.text: It pages two people at once
choices.why: Only in shadow and reverse shadow.

choices.text: It has been approved by the platform team and the director of engineering in writing
choices.why: Not the requirement in the lesson.

choices.text: It has a runbook page saying what it means and what to try first
choices.why: Right: the team now refuses to turn on an alert without one.

prompt: In Lucas’s first primary week, Diego was his named ___.
hint: Somebody who agreed to answer at any hour.

prompt: A new hire’s first week at a company: two days without a laptop, a list of documents to read, and a first task “to be decided once you know the code”. Which single change from this lesson would help most?

choices.text: Add more documents to the list
choices.why: Reading supports the goal; more of it does not replace the first change.

choices.text: Put the new hire on the on-call rota at once, so they learn the system quickly
choices.why: That skips the three steps the lesson says are needed.

choices.text: Shorten the first week
choices.why: The problem is what the week contains.

choices.text: Pick a small, real first task before day one, so that a change of theirs reaches production that week
choices.why: Right: the first change is the goal the rest of the week supports, and it needs to be chosen before day one.
